extracted.intended_audience: ARIPO patent examiners and patent applicants
extracted.subtask_description: Official guidelines for examining ARIPO patent applications, focusing on assessment of prior art (including internet disclosures), novelty, enabling disclosure, priority dates, and inventive step using established approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner response when applicant questions internet publication date
rubrics_metrics.description: If an applicant provides reasons for questioning the alleged publication date of an internet disclosure, examiners will have to take these reasons into account. If examiners are no longer convinced that the disclosure forms part of the state of the art, they will either have to present further evidence to maintain the disputed publication date or will not use this disclosure further as prior art against the application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The later the examiner sets out to obtain such evidence, the more difficult it may become. The examiner should use his judgment to decide whether it is worth spending a short amount of time at the search stage to find further evidence in support of the publication date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weight of unsubstantiated applicant assertions about internet reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: If an applicant refutes the publication date of an internet disclosure with no reasoning or merely with generic statements about the reliability of internet disclosures, this argument will be given minimal weight and is therefore unlikely to sway the examiner’s opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants must provide specific reasons/evidence; generic claims of unreliability are insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuum of reliability for internet disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: While the dates and content of internet disclosures can be taken at face value, there are differing degrees of reliability. The more reliable a disclosure, the harder it will be for the applicant to prove that it is incorrect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should assess reliability based on type/source of disclosure (see related categories: technical journals, print-equivalents, non-traditional publications).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of online technical journals
rubrics_metrics.description: Online technical journals from scientific publishers (e.g. IEEE, Springer, and Derwent) have the same reliability as traditional paper journals, i.e. very high.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note that internet publication of a journal issue may be earlier than the paper version; pre-published manuscripts should be treated as separate disclosures, each with its own publication date. If a given online journal date is too vague, the examiner may request the exact publication date (e.g. via publisher contact form or ARIPO library).

rubrics_metrics.name: Print-equivalent internet publications considered reliable
rubrics_metrics.description: Sources other than scientific publishers — e.g. newspapers, periodicals, television/radio stations, academic institutions, international organizations, public organizations, and standardization bodies — are generally deemed to provide reliable publication dates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Documents previously published on paper but now on the internet (manuals, product catalogues, white papers) are intended for the public and their given dates can usually be taken as publication dates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eprint archives and crawled repositories
rubrics_metrics.description: University-hosted eprint archives (e.g. arXiv.org, Cryptology eprint archive) and crawler-based repositories (e.g. Citeseer, ChemXseer) may contain preprints or archived materials; such archives are relevant prior art sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some archives crawl the internet automatically; archived items may be the only disclosure of content (pre-publication manuscripts). Treat archived/pre-published items as separate disclosures with their own dates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-traditional internet publications as prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Usenet discussion groups, blogs, e-mail archives of mailing lists or wiki pages also constitute prior art, although establishing their publication date may be more involved and their reliability may vary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Computer-generated timestamps (blogs, Usenet, wiki version history) can be considered reliable publication dates absent indications to the contrary. Frequently used “last modified” dates can be treated as publication dates in absence of contrary evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources of evidence for undated or unreliable internet disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an internet disclosure relevant for examination has no explicit publication date or a date has been shown unreliable, the examiner may try to obtain further evidence to establish or confirm the publication date using specified sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acceptable sources include: (a) internet archiving services (Wayback Machine), (b) version/history timestamps, (c) computer-generated file timestamps, (d) search-engine indexing dates (noting these are later than actual publication), (e) embedded date information recoverable by forensic tools (use only if examiner can explain how obtained), and (f) evidence of replication/mirror sites or statements from owners/authors (probative value assessed separately).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of undatable disclosures as prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: If no date can be obtained (other than the date of retrieval which is too late), the disclosure cannot be used as prior art during examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If highly relevant but undated, the examiner may cite it in the search report as an L document and must explain why it was cited; citing makes it citable against future applications using the date of retrieval as publication date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling framed pages, archived links and non-persistent URLs
rubrics_metrics.description: Web pages divided into frames may have content drawn from different sources with different publication dates; archived pages may have links to current versions; some URLs are non-persistent and only work for a session.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the cited publication date refers to the intended content. For non-persistent URLs or uncertain links, the examiner should indicate how the specific URL was reached from the site's home page (links followed or search terms used).

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical requirements for citing internet disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: When printing a web page, the complete URL and relevant publication date should be clearly legible; date formats vary (European dd/mm/yyyy, US mm/dd/yyyy, ISO yyyy/mm/dd) and can be ambiguous for days 1-12.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always indicate the date the web page was retrieved. When citing internet disclosures, explain prior art status and how/where the publication date was obtained (e.g., eight digits in URL represent YYYYMMDD), and relate multiple cited documents (e.g., which link leads to which document). Consider time zone when publication date is close to priority date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enabling disclosure requirement for public availability
rubrics_metrics.description: Subject-matter can only be regarded as having been made available to the public (and thus part of the state of the art) if the information given to the skilled person is sufficient to enable him, at the relevant date, to practice the technical teaching which is the subject of the disclosure, taking into account the general knowledge at that time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enablement is assessed at the relevant date and includes consideration of general knowledge expected of the skilled person.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective date: filing date or priority date per claim
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'date of filing' is to be interpreted as meaning the date of priority in appropriate cases. Different claims or alternatives in one claim may have different effective dates (filing or one of the claimed priority dates). The question of novelty must be considered against each claim (or part of a claim).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If all state-of-the-art matter was public before the earliest priority document, no allocation of effective dates is necessary. Late-filed missing parts get the date of filing of those elements unless fully contained in the priority document.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of earlier published applications in state of the art
rubrics_metrics.description: Other applications filed or validly claiming a priority date earlier than — but published on or after — the filing or valid date of priority of the application being examined, form part of the state of the art for novelty (but not inventive step). 'Content' includes description, drawings and claims, including explicit disclaimers (except for disclaimers for unworkable embodiments), references to other documents and prior art explicitly described.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'content' does not include any priority document (which serves only to determine priority validity). Whether a published application is a conflicting application depends on filing date and publication date and whether priority claims were valid at publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double patenting principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Two patents cannot be granted to the same applicant for one invention. It is permissible to allow two applications with the same description where the claims are distinct and directed to different inventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If two or more ARIPO applications from the same applicant definitively designate the same State(s) and claim the same invention, the applicant must amend to avoid claiming the same invention or choose which application to proceed to grant. If two applications of the same effective date come from different applicants, each proceeds as though the other did not exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict with national rights of earlier date and permissible amendments
rubrics_metrics.description: If a national right of earlier date exists in a designated Contracting State, the applicant may (i) withdraw that designation, (ii) file claims for that State different from other States, or (iii) limit claims so the national right is no longer relevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amendment to account for prior national rights should not be required or suggested, but where claims are amended, description/drawings should be amended if necessary to avoid confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty: prohibition on combining separate items of prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: In considering novelty (as distinct from inventive step), it is not permissible to combine separate items of prior art together, nor to combine separate items belonging to different embodiments described in the same document unless such combination has specifically been suggested.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a primary document explicitly refers to another document available to the public on the publication date, the teaching of the latter is regarded as incorporated into the primary document (relevant date remains that of the primary document). Matter explicitly disclaimed or prior art acknowledged in a document is regarded as incorporated in the document.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implicit features and well-known equivalents in novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: A document takes away the novelty of any claimed subject-matter derivable directly and unambiguously from that document including features implicit to a person skilled in the art. However, it is not correct to interpret the teaching document as embracing well-known equivalents not disclosed; that is a matter of obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether subject-matter is 'derivable directly and unambiguously' from the document; implicit but inevitable consequences can destroy novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevant date for reading a prior document
rubrics_metrics.description: In determining novelty, a prior document should be read as it would have been read by a person skilled in the art on the relevant date: the publication date for previously published documents and the date of filing (or priority date where appropriate) for documents under Section 3(2)(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation must reflect the skilled person's perspective at that date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic disclosure vs specific examples in novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: A generic disclosure does not usually take away the novelty of any specific example within that disclosure, but a specific disclosure does take away the novelty of a generic claim embracing that disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: disclosure of copper takes away novelty of 'metal' as a generic concept but not the novelty of other metals; disclosure of rivets takes away novelty of 'fastening means' as a generic concept but not other fastening types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implicit disclosure and parameterised claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Lack of novelty may be implicit in that, in carrying out the teaching of the prior document, the skilled person would inevitably arrive at a result falling within the claim. Such an objection should be raised only where there can be no reasonable doubt as to the practical effect of the prior teaching.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For parameter-defined claims, examiner should consider whether applicant's evidence (e.g., comparison tests) shows differences; otherwise question whether the application actually discloses essential features to achieve claimed parameters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examination of novelty: disregard of non-distinctive use characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: In determining novelty, the examiner should remember that, particularly for claims directed to a physical entity, non-distinctive characteristics of a particular intended use should be disregarded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a claim to substance X 'for use as a catalyst' not novel over same substance known as a dye unless the use implies a particular form distinguishing it from the known form. For first medical use, a claim to a known compound for a particular purpose based on a technical effect is interpreted as including that technical effect as a functional technical feature and is not objectionable under Section 3(10)(b) provided the feature was not previously made available to the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection invention novelty (two-lists principle and selections)
rubrics_metrics.description: Selection inventions involve selecting individual elements, sub-sets, or sub-ranges not explicitly mentioned within a larger known set/range. A selection from a single list of specifically disclosed elements does not confer novelty. However, selection from two or more lists of a certain length to arrive at a specific combination not specifically disclosed confers novelty (two-lists principle).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include selection of chemical compounds from generic formulas (selecting substituents from two+ lists), starting materials for manufacturing, and sub-ranges of parameters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty of selected sub-ranges (three criteria)
rubrics_metrics.description: A sub-range selected from a broader known numerical range is considered novel if: (a) the selected sub-range is narrow compared to the known range; (b) it is sufficiently far removed from any specific examples disclosed in the prior art and from the end-points of the known range; and (c) the selected range is not an arbitrary specimen of the prior art but another invention (purposive selection, new technical teaching).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An effect occurring only in the claimed sub-range cannot by itself confer novelty, but may confirm criterion (c). 'Narrow' and 'sufficiently far removed' are decided case-by-case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty assessment for overlapping ranges and chemical formulae
rubrics_metrics.description: For overlapping ranges (numerical or chemical), novelty is destroyed by an explicitly mentioned end-point, intermediate values or specific examples in the overlap. For overlapping chemical formulae, novelty is acknowledged if the claimed subject-matter is distinguished in the overlap by a new technical element (e.g., a specifically selected residue not individualized in the prior art).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the whole content of the prior art document and whether the skilled person would seriously contemplate applying the prior teaching in the range of overlap; apply the sub-range criteria analogously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-prejudicial disclosures (exceptions to state of the art)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two specific instances where a prior disclosure is not taken into account as part of the state of the art: (i) disclosure due to or in consequence of an evident abuse in relation to the applicant or legal predecessor; (ii) display of the invention by the applicant at an officially recognized international exhibition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the only two instances. Time limit: disclosure must have taken place not earlier than six months preceding filing of the ARIPO application (relevant date is actual filing date, not priority date).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evident abuse conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: For 'evident abuse' there must be on the part of the discloser either actual intent to cause harm or actual or constructive knowledge that harm would or could ensue from the disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An example: B discloses A's invention despite a confidential disclosure; A can apply within six months of such publication and not be prejudiced.

rubrics_metrics.name: International exhibition non-prejudice conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: If the invention was displayed at a recognized international exhibition, the application must be filed within six months of the display to avoid prejudice; the applicant must state at filing that the invention was so displayed and must file a supporting certificate within four months giving required particulars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognized exhibitions are published in the Official Journal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive step general test
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention involves an inventive step if, having regard to the state of the art, it is not obvious to a person skilled in the art. The question arises only if the invention is novel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Novelty and inventive step are different criteria; assess inventive step only after novelty established.

rubrics_metrics.name: State of the art for inventive step (including common general knowledge)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'state of the art' for inventive step concerns information relevant to a field of technology and may reside in the relevant common general knowledge, which need not be in writing and needs substantiation only if challenged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider common general knowledge in the relevant field when assessing inventive step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of the person skilled in the art
rubrics_metrics.description: The person skilled in the art is presumed to be a skilled practitioner in the relevant field, possessed of average knowledge and ability and aware of what was common general knowledge at the relevant date; he should be presumed to have access to everything in the state of the art and to have normal means for routine work and experimentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the problem prompts seeking solutions in another technical field, the specialist in that field is the person qualified. Assessment may sometimes be in terms of a group (research/production team). The skilled person has same level of skill for assessing inventive step and sufficiency of disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness test and temporal scope of knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: The question is whether, before the filing/priority date valid for the claim, having regard to the art known at the time, it would have been obvious to the person skilled in the art to arrive at something within the claim. 'Obvious' means something not going beyond normal technological progress and not involving skill beyond that expected of the skilled person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In considering inventive step, construe any published document in the light of knowledge up to and including the day before the filing/priority date and regard all knowledge generally available to the skilled person up to that day.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem-and-solution approach for inventive step
rubrics_metrics.description: To assess inventive step in an objective and predictable manner, the problem-and-solution approach should be applied (deviation should be exceptional). The approach has three main stages: (i) determining the closest prior art, (ii) establishing the objective technical problem to be solved, and (iii) considering whether the claimed invention, starting from the closest prior art and the objective technical problem, would have been obvious to the skilled person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the three-stage problem-and-solution framework to ensure predictable, objective inventive-step assessments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of the closest prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: The closest prior art is that single reference disclosing the combination of features which constitutes the most promising starting point for an obvious development leading to the invention. It should be directed to a similar purpose/effect or at least belong to the same or a closely related technical field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In practice, the closest prior art corresponds to a similar use and requires the minimum structural and functional modifications to arrive at the claimed invention. Assess from the skilled person's point of view as of the day before filing/priority date. Take account of what the applicant acknowledges as known unless applicant corrects it.
